advances:
A compatible common core gives an explicit continuous log-concave output at one integral fiber, with aggregate source marginals dominated as measures by the original stocks. The actual output centroid has mixed-integer depth at least the output mass divided by \(e\). Every coupling uses original partial stocks directly; no output is reused as a source.

The box family below yields output mass at least \((3/7)2^{-n}W\), even though the normalized output has relative entropy at least \(n\log(3/2)\) with respect to the original target-fiber uniform law. Thus this construction does not require a bounded-entropy comparison with that law.

No universal retained-mass floor for arbitrary convex bodies is proved. To obtain the locked target by this common-core mechanism, a further geometric theorem would need to provide a compatible core and reflection-invariant source set for which \(k_E\mathcal L^d(K)\) has a dimension-independent lower bound of order \(2^{-n}W\). That existence claim remains open.

proof:
Choose \(\mathbf q\in\operatorname{int}K\). To make the density continuous even at its support boundary, define
\[
p_K(\mathbf v)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbf v\in t(K-\mathbf q)\},
\qquad
g(\mathbf x)=\min\{1,\,2d(1-p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q))_+\},
\tag{6}
\]
where \(s_+=\max\{s,0\}\). The gauge \(p_K\) is finite, convex, and continuous. Indeed, \(K-\mathbf q\) contains an origin-centered ball of some radius \(r>0\). Convexity gives subadditivity and positive homogeneity of the gauge, whence
\(p_K(\mathbf v)-p_K(\mathbf w)\le p_K(\mathbf v-\mathbf w)\le\|\mathbf v-\mathbf w\|/r\), together with the reverse bound obtained by interchanging \(\mathbf v,\mathbf w\). Compactness and the definition of the gauge give \(K-\mathbf q=\{\mathbf v:p_K(\mathbf v)\le1\}\). Moreover, its interior is \(\{p_K<1\}\): a strict sublevel point is interior by continuity, whereas an interior point can be slightly expanded radially while staying in \(K-\mathbf q\). Thus the gauge equals one on the boundary.

It follows that \(g\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R^d\), vanishes outside \(K\) and on its boundary, satisfies \(0\le g\le\mathbf1_K\), and is positive in \(\operatorname{int}K\). On \(K\), it is the minimum of the constant function one and the nonnegative concave function \(2d(1-p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q))\). This minimum is concave because its hypograph is the intersection of their convex hypographs. Nonnegative concavity on a convex set implies log-concavity there, by the concavity inequality followed by weighted arithmetic-geometric mean. When either endpoint value is zero, the log-concavity inequality for a weight strictly between zero and one has right side zero. The zero extension is therefore log-concave on all of \(\mathbb R^d\).

Put \(G=\int g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\). The density equals one on \(\mathbf q+(1-1/(2d))(K-\mathbf q)\), so Bernoulli's inequality gives
\[
0<G\le\mathcal L^d(K),
\qquad
G\ge\left(1-\frac1{2d}\right)^d\mathcal L^d(K)
\ge\frac12\mathcal L^d(K).
\tag{7}
\]

Partition \(E\) into its reflection orbits. Its only possible fixed point is \(\mathbf J\), so the orbit count is exactly \(k_E\). For a two-element orbit \(\{\mathbf I,\mathbf I'\}\), where \(\mathbf I'=2\mathbf J-\mathbf I\), push the finite measure \(g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\) forward under the two-source map
\[
\mathbf x\longmapsto
\bigl(\mathbf b+A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)+\mathbf x,
      \mathbf b+A(\mathbf I'-\mathbf J)+\mathbf x\bigr).
\tag{8}
\]
Condition (1) places each coordinate in its original source fiber. Give the sources barycentric coefficients \(1/2,1/2\). This is a finite source coupling of mass \(G\), not a coupling with prescribed uniform marginals. Linearity of \(A\) and the reflection identity show that its continuous output is \(\mathbf b+\mathbf x\) and its base output is \(\mathbf J\). If \(\mathbf J\in E\), its singleton orbit gives the one-source coupling obtained by pushing \(g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\) forward under \(\mathbf x\mapsto\mathbf b+\mathbf x\), with barycentric coefficient one. This has the same mass and output law.

The actual marginal at each \(\mathbf I\in E\) is
\[
d\nu_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf y)
=g\bigl(\mathbf y-\mathbf b-A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)\bigr)\,d\mathbf y
\le\mathbf1_{C_{\mathbf I}}(\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y
=d\mu_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf y).
\tag{9}
\]
The inequality follows pointwise from (1) and \(g\le\mathbf1_K\); translation has Jacobian one. The reflection orbits partition \(E\), so no index is charged by two couplings. At indices outside \(E\), the aggregate marginal is zero. Hence (9) proves aggregate domination as measures by the original stocks, not just a scalar capacity bound. No output measure is used as an input to another coupling.

Convexity of \(C\) gives \(\mathbf b+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\). For a pair and any \(\mathbf x\in K\), the midpoint of the two ambient source points in (8) is \((\mathbf J,\mathbf b+\mathbf x)\). For the singleton, the inclusion is already (1). Since \(E\) is nonempty, at least one argument applies. In particular, \(w_{\mathbf J}\ge\mathcal L^d(K)>0\), so \(\mathbf J\in D\). Summing the \(k_E\) identical output laws gives
\[
d\kappa_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf y)
=k_Eg(\mathbf y-\mathbf b)\,d\mathbf y,
\qquad M=k_EG.
\tag{10}
\]
The density is nonzero, continuous, log-concave, and supported in \(\mathbf b+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\). Equation (7) proves (2).

For completeness, fix a proper closed ambient halfspace
\(H=\{(\mathbf z,\mathbf y):\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf z\rangle+\langle\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf y\rangle\ge t\}\), where \((\mathbf a,\boldsymbol\beta)\ne(\mathbf0,\mathbf0)\). If a barycentric output is in \(H\), at least one source point is in \(H\). Otherwise every source score is strictly below \(t\), and their barycentric average is strictly below \(t\), a contradiction. For a singleton, the source and output events coincide. Integrating this event inequality over each coupling, summing the orbits, and using (9) yields
\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}(H_{\mathbf J})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\nu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\mu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H).
\]
Zero-volume fibers contribute zero to the last sum. This proves (3), including closed-boundary events and vertical halfspaces. If the whole space is admitted as a halfspace, the same event inequality applies to it as well.

Set \(\rho=\delta_{\mathbf J}\otimes\kappa_{\mathbf J}\), where \(\delta_{\mathbf J}\) is the unit point mass. It is nonzero and compactly supported, and its density relative to its affine support \(\{\mathbf J\}\times\mathbb R^d\) is the log-concave density in (10). Thus it is a log-concave measure, using the affine-support characterization recorded in accepted fact f049539ffd9c9b1d. Its base projection is \(M\delta_{\mathbf J}\), so every projected closed halfspace containing \(\mathbf J\) has full mass \(M\). Apply that accepted fact with \(z_0=\mathbf J\) and \(\alpha=1\). The selected submeasure has the same mass as \(\rho\) and is dominated by it, hence equals \(\rho\). Therefore every closed ambient halfspace containing the barycenter \((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star)\) of \(\rho\) has \(\rho\)-mass at least \(M/e\). The centroid belongs to the compact convex set \(\mathbf b+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\). Combining the bound with (3) gives \(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star))\ge M/e\) at that one fixed point.

We now verify the example (4). Each condition \(z_i^2\le y_i\) is a convex epigraph condition. Together with \(y_i\le3\), these conditions define a closed convex bounded set: \(|z_i|\le\sqrt3\) and \(0\le y_i\le3\). The point \(\mathbf z=\mathbf0\), \(\mathbf y=(3/2)\mathbf1_N\) satisfies all inequalities strictly, so \(C_N\) has nonempty interior and is a convex body. Its entire nonempty lattice-fiber support is \(D_N=\{-1,0,1\}^N\), and every such fiber has positive volume. With the preceding notation applied to \(C_N\),
\[
(C_N)_{\mathbf I}=\prod_{i=1}^N[I_i^2,3],
\qquad
w_{\mathbf I}=\prod_{i=1}^N(3-I_i^2),
\qquad
W=\prod_{i=1}^N(2+3+2)=7^N.
\tag{11}
\]
There are no further nonempty lattice fibers, even of zero volume. Every displayed fiber contains \(K=[1,3]^N\).

Choose \(E=D_N\), \(\mathbf J=\mathbf0\), \(\mathbf b=\mathbf0\), \(A=0\), and \(\mathbf q=2\mathbf1_N\). Then (1) holds, \(k_E=(3^N+1)/2\), and \(\mathcal L^N(K)=2^N\). The gauge in (6) is \(p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q)=\max_i|x_i-2|\). Consequently the output density is invariant under reflection of each coordinate about two, so its centroid is \(2\mathbf1_N\). Equations (7) and (10) give the first inequality in (5). For the second,
\[
\frac{2^NM}{W}
\ge\frac14\left[\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)^N
                     +\left(\frac47\right)^N\right]
\ge\frac14\frac{12}{7}=\frac37,
\]
because \(N\ge1\) and \(12/7>1\).

Finally, let \(U_K=2^{-N}\mathcal L^N|_K\), an auxiliary core law distinct from the original fiber laws. The original target law is \(U_{\mathbf0}=3^{-N}\mathcal L^N|_{[0,3]^N}\). Equation (10) gives \(P=g\,d\mathbf x/G\). This probability law is supported in \(K\) and has bounded density. Its density ratios with respect to both uniform laws are bounded, so both entropies below are finite, using the convention \(0\log0=0\). Taking the density ratio on \(K\) yields
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_{\mathbf0})
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_K)+N\log(3/2)
\ge N\log(3/2).
\]
The last inequality is Jensen's inequality for \(s\log s\) under \(U_K\), since \(\int(dP/dU_K)\,dU_K=1\). Thus the log-concave output retains the stated mass without a dimension-independent relative-entropy bound with respect to the original target-fiber uniform law.
statement:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body. Use the canonical notation of accepted fact 793210f8a4be3647: \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\), \(S=C\cap\Lambda\), and, for every \(\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n\),
\[
C_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^d:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in C\},
\qquad
\mu_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}},
\qquad
w_{\mathbf I}=|\mu_{\mathbf I}|.
\]
Put \(D=\{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\) and \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal H_d(S)\), and assume \(W>0\). The set \(D\) is finite. For \(\mathbf I\in D\), put \(U_{\mathbf I}=\mu_{\mathbf I}/w_{\mathbf I}\). For \(\mathbf p\in S\), let \(h_S(\mathbf p)\) be the infimum of \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\) over all closed ambient halfspaces \(H\) containing \(\mathbf p\), as in the locked problem. All logarithms are natural.

Suppose \(\mathbf J\in\mathbb Z^n\), \(E\subseteq D\) is nonempty and satisfies \(2\mathbf J-E=E\), \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body, \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^d\) is a linear map such that
\[
\mathbf b+A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf I}
\qquad(\mathbf I\in E).
\tag{1}
\]
Let \(k_E=(|E|+\mathbf1_{\{\mathbf J\in E\}})/2\), the number of reflection orbits in \(E\). There is one finite source coupling per orbit: a two-source coupling with barycentric coefficients \(1/2,1/2\) for a two-element orbit, or a one-source coupling with coefficient one for the possible singleton \(\{\mathbf J\}\). Each coupling has integral base barycenter \(\mathbf J\). Its output is the pushforward under the corresponding barycentric average of the ambient source points.

The aggregate output measure \(\kappa_{\mathbf J}\) has a nonzero continuous log-concave Lebesgue density on \(\mathbb R^d\), is supported in \(C_{\mathbf J}\), and has mass
\[
M:=|\kappa_{\mathbf J}|\ge\frac{k_E}{2}\mathcal L^d(K).
\tag{2}
\]
At every original index, the sum of the actual source marginal measures of all couplings is dominated by \(\mu_{\mathbf I}\). Each index in \(E\) is used in exactly one coupling, and no other index is used.

For every closed ambient halfspace \(H\), put \(H_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in H\}\). Then
\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}(H_{\mathbf J})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\mu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H).
\tag{3}
\]
Consequently the actual output centroid \(\mathbf y^\star=M^{-1}\int\mathbf y\,d\kappa_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf y)\) satisfies \((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star)\in S\) and \(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star))\ge M/e\). This uses the centroid consequence of accepted fact f049539ffd9c9b1d on the chosen integral fiber, rather than a centroid of an original uniform fiber law.

In particular, for every integer \(N\ge1\), let \(n=d=N\), write \(\mathbf1_N=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^N\), and set
\[
C_N=\{(\mathbf z,\mathbf y)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N:
                z_i^2\le y_i\le3\ (1\le i\le N)\}.
\tag{4}
\]
At \(\mathbf J=\mathbf0\), the construction can be chosen to have a continuous log-concave output supported in \([1,3]^N\), with centroid \(2\mathbf1_N\), original source marginal domination, and
\[
M\ge2^{N-2}(3^N+1)
\ge\frac37\,2^{-N}W,
\qquad W=7^N.
\tag{5}
\]
For its normalized output \(P=\kappa_{\mathbf0}/M\) and the original target law \(U_{\mathbf0}\), with the normalization of accepted fact 793210f8a4be3647, one nevertheless has \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_{\mathbf0})\ge N\log(3/2)\). Here \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\int\log(dP/dQ)\,dP\) when \(P\ll Q\).
